title: Zechariah 12:10–14
context: The LORD promises to pour on David’s house and the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of supplication. They will look to the one whom they have pierced and mourn as for an only son, with a mourning compared to that of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddo. The land will mourn family by family: David’s house, Nathan’s, Levi’s, the Shimeites, and all the rest, the men and their wives apart. The verse moves from me to him in speaking of the pierced one, and these notes leave that wording as it stands. John 19:37 cites this verse at the crucifixion: “They will look on him whom they pierced.” Revelation 1:7 echoes it; these uses are named without being merged with Zechariah. Both traditions see here God’s gracious work bringing his people to repentance; they differ on whether that grace enables a response that can be refused or effectually renews the heart, as the notes on 12:10 explain.

verses.text: I will pour on David’s house and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of supplication. They will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him as one grieves for his firstborn.
verses.arminianNotes: I will pour on David’s house and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of supplication. Arminian readers see grace enabling a response that can be refused, as the John 6:44 box describes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see grace that effectually renews, compare Ezekiel 36:26; the Philippians 2:13 box sets out both readings. John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 echo the pierced one; the verse moves from me to him.

verses.text: In that day there will be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddo.
verses.arminianNotes: In that day there will be a great mourning in Jerusalem, Arminian readers see a national grief so deep that it recalls the most famous mourning in Israel’s memory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many connect Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddo with the mourning for Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:22-25), though the meaning of the name is uncertain.

verses.text: The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of David’s house apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart;
verses.arminianNotes: The land will mourn, every family apart; Arminian readers see repentance that reaches every household, beginning with the family of David’s house and their wives apart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the house of Nathan may be David’s son (2 Samuel 5:14; Luke 3:31) or the prophet Nathan; readers differ. Royal and prophetic lines alike are named.

verses.text: the family of the house of Levi apart, and their wives apart; the family of the Shimeites apart, and their wives apart;
verses.arminianNotes: the family of the house of Levi apart, Arminian readers see the priestly families joining the mourning, each with their wives apart, so that the leaders of worship also repent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the family of the Shimeites matches Numbers 3:21, a Levite family descended from Gershon, though some suggest another Shimei. The identification is uncertain.

verses.text: all the families who remain, every family apart, and their wives apart.
verses.arminianNotes: all the families who remain, every family apart, and their wives apart. Arminian readers see the mourning extended to every remaining family, a repentance shared by the whole people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repetition of apart stresses personal, household repentance. Shared ground: both traditions see true mourning for sin as both corporate and individual.
